chunks: "The body diode conducts during the dead time at about 0. 7 to 1 volts, and that has five consequences I'd design around.
One, loss: V SD times I times t dead times f , plus reverse recovery.

At 12 volts in, 2 amps and 500 kilohertz with 50 nanoseconds of total dead time per cycle, 25 at each of the two edges, that's about 40 milliwatts of conduction, but 20 nC of recovery charge is another 120 milliwatts, so recovery usually matters more as V in and frequency go up.
Two, dead-time setting: it has to be long enough to avoid shoot-through across delay mismatch and temperature, and no longer, because every extra nanosecond costs diode loss and charge.
That pushes toward adaptive dead time. Three, the negative voltage on SW.
The controller's SW or phase pin must tolerate about minus one diode drop plus undershoot, or it can latch up through its substrate. I'd check the absolute maximum rating.
When the high side turns on and the diode snaps off, the recovery current flows in loop inductance and rings, producing overshoot on SW and noise at 100 megahertz or more.
I'd think about layout, gate resistance or a snubber.
Five, the diode's current and thermal rating, and temperature drift: V SD drops with temperature, and the diode must carry the peak inductor current.
And for device selection I'd pick a FET with low Q rr ."
